head: An old family inn
became a resort doctor.
slides.sub: How Hoshino Resorts learned to run hotels it doesn’t own.

image.label: A wooden hot spring inn in a misty forest
image.brief: 안개 낀 숲속의 오래된 일본 목조 온천 여관. 김이 오르는 노천탕, 고요하고 영화 같은 톤. 로고·간판 문자 없음.

head: A forest town
and a family business.
body: The Hoshino family began doing business in Karuizawa, a cool mountain town northwest of Tokyo, in 1904. Over the decades it became known for its hot spring inn.
For most of the century, the job was simple: look after one place, and look after it well.

image.label: A quiet mountain town street in early 20th-century Japan
image.brief: 20세기 초 일본 산간 마을 거리. 목조 건물과 흙길, 낙엽송 숲. 세피아 톤.

slides.label: generation of the family to lead the company, from 1991
body: Yoshiharu Hoshino took over in 1991 after studying hotel management in the United States. He found an old-fashioned business that struggled to keep and hire young staff.

image.label: A young manager silhouetted in an empty inn lobby
image.brief: 텅 빈 여관 로비에 선 젊은 경영자의 실루엣. 얼굴은 보이지 않게. 1990년대 초 분위기.

head: He flattened the company
and let staff decide.
body: Hoshino reportedly ran the inn by the textbook he trusted: fewer layers, open debate, and staff who suggest ideas instead of waiting for orders.
Workers also learned several jobs. The same person might check guests in, clean rooms and serve dinner, moving to wherever the work was.

image.label: Inn staff in uniforms discussing around a low table
image.brief: 유니폼 차림의 여관 직원들이 낮은 탁자에 둘러앉아 토론하는 장면. 일반적인 인물, 얼굴은 흐릿하게.

head: Then the bubble burst.
Resorts began to fail.
body: In the late 1980s, Japan built resorts, ski hills and golf hotels at a furious pace. When the bubble economy collapsed in the early 1990s, many were left with debt and empty rooms.
Their owners and banks needed someone who could actually run them.

image.label: A large empty resort hotel under grey skies
image.brief: 흐린 하늘 아래 텅 빈 대형 리조트 호텔. 꺼진 간판, 빈 주차장. 1990년대 일본.

head: A failing resort is offered.
What do you do?
body: You run one well-loved inn. A big, struggling resort far from home wants help.

options.text: Buy the building and rebuild it as your own luxury property
options.feedback: You control everything, but you take on huge debt and can only do this a few times. Keep swiping.

options.text: Say no and stay focused on the inn you know
options.feedback: Safe and calm. But the skills you built would stay locked in one town. Keep swiping.

options.text: Run it for the owner, keep the staff, and rethink the concept with them
options.feedback: This is the path Hoshino took. It means earning results without owning the asset. Keep swiping.

image.label: A key and a contract on a wooden desk
image.brief: 나무 책상 위의 열쇠 하나와 계약서. 창밖으로 눈 덮인 산과 리조트.

head: Same building, same staff.
A new reason to visit.
body: Around 2001, Hoshino began taking over the operation of struggling resorts, starting with one in Kobuchizawa, Yamanashi.
Instead of firing teams, it brought its flat style and multitasking. Local staff helped decide what each place should stand for, often built around the region’s own food and scenery.

image.label: Hotel staff preparing a local-themed dining hall
image.brief: 지역 특색을 살린 식당을 준비하는 리조트 직원들. 따뜻한 조명, 지역 식재료. 실존 인물 얼굴 없음.

slides.label: hotels and resorts operated by Hoshino Resorts, according to the company
body: The family rebuilt its own inn as the upscale HOSHINOYA Karuizawa in 2005. Other brands followed, from hot spring ryokan to city hotels, many in buildings it does not own.

image.label: A map of Japan dotted with small lights
image.brief: 작은 불빛이 점점이 찍힌 일본 지도. 어두운 배경, 따뜻한 빛.

head: Owners hold the buildings.
Hoshino runs them.
body: In 2013, a separate real estate fund, Hoshino Resorts REIT, was listed to own hotel properties. Hoshino Resorts focused on what it did best: operating.
That split let it grow without carrying every building’s debt.

image.label: A hotel building split into blueprint and lit interior
image.brief: 한쪽은 설계도, 한쪽은 불 켜진 객실로 나뉜 호텔 건물 그래픽.

head: Own the know-how,
not the buildings.
body: Hotels are usually asset-heavy. Hoshino turned its real strength, a way of running places with motivated, flexible staff, into something it could carry from resort to resort.
Owners supplied the buildings. Hoshino supplied the people system that made them work.

image.label: A single lantern being passed between hands
image.brief: 손에서 손으로 건네지는 등불 하나. 어두운 배경, 인물은 손만 보이게.

head: Your best asset may be
how you run things.
body: A method that works in one place can work in many, if you separate it from the bricks.
**Try it today:** write down what you do better than others. Could you offer it to someone who owns what you don’t?

image.label: A lit inn window glowing at night in the forest
image.brief: 밤 숲속에서 따뜻하게 빛나는 여관 창문 하나.

factChecks.note: 호시노 가문의 가루이자와 사업 시작(1904년)과 온천 여관 개업(1914년)은 Hoshino Resorts 공식 연혁으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 1904년만 적었습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1904년 가루이자와 임업으로 시작, 1914년 첫 온천 여관 확인.
호시노 요시하루가 4대째 경영자이며 1991년 사장에 취임했고, 미국 코넬대 호텔경영대학원에서 공부했다는 내용은 회사 연혁과 주요 인터뷰 기준입니다. 학위 명칭은 카드에 넣지 않았습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 호시노 요시하루 4대째 확인. 1991년 취임은 이번 검색에서 직접 확인되지 않음(1995년 사명 변경 확인).
취임 초기 직원 이탈과 채용난, 수평적 조직과 '멀티태스킹'(한 직원이 프런트·객실·식당을 함께 맡는 방식) 도입은 여러 인터뷰와 사례 연구에 나오는 내용입니다. 구체적인 이직률 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
2001년 무렵 야마나시현 고부치자와 리조트(현 Risonare Yatsugatake) 운영을 맡은 것이 재생 사업의 시작이라는 점은 회사 연혁으로 확인하세요. 당시 소유주 이름은 넣지 않았습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] 2001년 RISONARE Yatsugatake(고부치자와 지역) 운영 시작 확인.
"60+" 시설 수는 회사 발표 기준이며 시점에 따라 달라집니다. 최신 공식 자료로 확인하고 필요하면 수정하세요. 카드에 "according to the company"로 표시했습니다.
HOSHINOYA 가루이자와 개업(2005년)과 Hoshino Resorts REIT 상장(2013년)은 회사 연혁과 도쿄증권거래소 자료로 확인하세요. → [2026-11-02 확인] 2005년 HOSHINOYA 가루이자와, 2013년 Hoshino Resorts REIT 상장 확인.
버블 붕괴 후 많은 리조트가 경영난에 빠졌다는 설명은 정성적으로만 적었고, 리조트법 등 구체적 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
